samba.d: Rio's Black communities fused African drum patterns, call-and-response and European harmony into carnival parade music, dense percussion layers on a two-beat pulse driving the whole body to sway.

bossa-nova.d: Rio's middle class slowed and simplified samba, adding jazz harmony and breathy vocals, guitar syncopation pushing gently like a wave, quiet and languid.

mpb.d: During the military dictatorship, Brazilian musicians stewed bossa nova, samba and folk rock into politically sharp singer-songwriter music where lyrics come before rhythm.

tango.d: Immigrant music from the port districts of Buenos Aires: bandoneón and strings strike a melancholy yet hard gait, while couples dance pressed close, resisting and supporting each other.

forro.d: Dance music of Brazil's northeastern drylands, accordion, triangle and zabumba drum holding up brisk two- and three-beat rhythms, singing of drought, migration and longing.

sertanejo.d: It began as rural folk song in inland São Paulo, two acoustic guitars and falsetto duets; plugged in during the 1990s, it became Brazil's best-selling popular music.

bachata.d: The Dominican Republic's rural guitar heartbreak song, bongos and güira behind a bright high-pitched guitar, telling of betrayal and longing, a low-class label turned global romance.

merengue.d: The Dominican national dance, tambora drum and güira driving a two-beat while brass stabs press down, the whole room dragging its steps left and right.

kompa.d: Port-au-Prince, Haiti put local rhythms into electric guitar, brass and congas: a gentle, restrained sway, the elegant version of Caribbean urban dance music.

calypso.d: Trinidad's carnival improvised satire song, steel drums and guitar carrying the narrative lilt of the West Indies, delivering both news and jokes.

soca.d: Calypso sped up and stuffed with drum machines and synths, the accent landing on the kick drum, building tireless propulsion for the carnival procession.

zouk.d: Musicians from Guadeloupe and Martinique stacked kompa, local drumming and synths into a dense dance music, the drum kit busy, the vocals sweet but tough.

kizomba.d: Angolans slowed zouk down further and stirred in semba's close body rhythm, the drums lingering; it is called Africa's slow-dance love song.

dembow.d: Jamaican dancehall's tresillo drum pattern, looped, sampled, sped up and stacked by Puerto Ricans, became the skeletal rhythm of reggaeton.

moombahton.d: A Washington, DC producer dropped the dembow rhythm to 108 BPM and laid house bass under it: a hybrid slow enough to grind to and still jump to.

nu-cumbia.d: Electronic artists in Argentina and Mexico stitched sampled cumbia accordion, synths and dancefloor bass together, nostalgic and jittery at once.

juju.d: Yoruba guitar-band music, several guitars interweaving into conversational melody lines, with talking drums and a choir, a thick yet loose texture.

fuji.d: The big-band music Lagos's Muslim community built from apala and sakara, drumming extremely dense, lead vocal and chorus trading back and forth.

soukous.d: Two Congolese guitars broke rumba into alternating repeated phrases while the drum kit pushed on; in the 1980s it leapt from Kinshasa to Paris dancehalls.

makossa.d: The festival dance music of Douala: bass carrying its own melody, brass in unison, hard drums; in the 1970s Dibango carried it to the world.

mbalax.d: Senegal's Wolof rhythm, sabar drums hammering densely alongside guitar and brass, the vocals high and strident, all the dancing driven from waist and belly.

taarab.d: Wedding music of coastal Zanzibar, Arabic melody, Indian strings and African drums jumbled together, the singing long and sweetly turned, with words that matter.

benga.d: Kenya's Luo people moved the phrasing of the traditional lyre onto guitar and bass, a light, leaping rhythm, the most popular local sound around independence.

chimurenga.d: The sound of resistance in Rhodesian times: mbira patterns transferred to guitar, hoarse vocals and political lyrics; the name means 'revolution'.

kuduro.d: It grew out of Luanda's neighbourhoods after Angola's civil war, fast electronic beats with rough rapping and improvised dance steps; the name means 'hard ass'.

coupe-decale.d: Invented by DJ circles during Côte d'Ivoire's civil conflict: drums cut sharp, slogan-like shout-along vocals, exaggerated dance moves, built purely for party release.
